title: Why We Should Fight
gist: Kori Schake traces the Powell Doctrine to Weinberger's 1984 six tests and argues Trump's February 2026 war on Iran fails every one of them — no clear objectives, no congressional authorization, no exhausted diplomacy, no exit strategy, no allied consultation — with the Strait of Hormuz closure, $37.5 billion to $50-plus billion in costs and an $88 billion supplemental request as the price. She predicts the U.S. emerges politically and militarily weaker and less trusted, and argues congressional appropriations leverage is the only realistic corrective.

themes.theme: Origins and content of the Powell Doctrine

insights.claim: The Powell Doctrine originated not in the Gulf War but in the 1983 Beirut barracks bombing that killed 241 U.S. service members, after which Reagan withdrew forces and Weinberger set out to prevent a repeat.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Doctrines that constrain force emerge from defeats, so a costly Iran outcome is the historical precondition for the next restraint framework.
insights.locator: In foreign policy, good ideas often emerge

insights.claim: Weinberger's November 1984 speech set six tests for using force: vital national interests at stake, willingness to commit resources for victory, clearly defined political and military objectives, continual reassessment of deployments and objectives, public and congressional support obtained through candor, and force as a last resort.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: A concrete six-item checklist any observer can run against a live military operation to forecast its likely failure modes.
insights.quote: the commitment of U.S. forces to combat should be a last resort.
insights.locator: In his speech, delivered in November 1984

insights.claim: Powell added two conditions to Weinberger's list — a clear exit strategy and international support — and defined the ideal exit as victory, meaning the adversary concedes the political objectives the war was fought over.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Defining victory as adversary concession, not target destruction, is the standard by which the current Iran campaign is judged to have no achievable endpoint.
insights.locator: Once Bush decided to use force

insights.claim: Because chance shapes war outcomes heavily, ensuring victory requires a wide margin for error, which Powell translated into the requirement for 'decisive force.'
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Explains why incrementalism and flexibility, praised as Trumpian virtues, are structurally war-losing choices under this framework.
insights.locator: And because chance shapes outcomes in war

insights.claim: Powell became a central player in the marginalization of his own doctrine, executing the Afghanistan and Iraq wars as secretary of state despite neither meeting his criteria, and the 'Pottery Barn rule' caution does not exculpate him.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Institutional guardrails erode from within by their own authors, which is why doctrine without a statutory enforcement mechanism decays.
insights.quote: you break it, you own it

insights.claim: The doctrine was designed to restrain civilian leaders from using force simply to 'do something' and to ensure force is rarely employed and always integrated with other elements of national power.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: The Albright-Powell exchange captures the perennial tension between capability and restraint that recurs in every intervention debate.
insights.quote: What’s the point of having this superb military that you’re always talking about if we can’t use it?

insights.claim: The author's core position is that despite its critics and Powell's own inconsistency, the doctrine remains the best available decision framework for American presidents contemplating war.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Signals where the mainstream Republican national-security establishment, via AEI, is anchoring its critique of the administration.

themes.theme: How the Iran war fails every test

insights.claim: Trump launched the February 2026 war on Iran without delineated objectives, without consulting Congress or allies other than Israel, without an authorization for the use of military force, without exhausting diplomacy or economic coercion, and without an exit strategy.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: A five-way failure against the doctrine's tests, which the author uses to explain why the campaign is producing compounding rather than converging outcomes.
insights.locator: In late February, Trump launched a war on Iran

insights.claim: Trump's February 28 pre-taped announcement listed so many objectives — destroying missiles, annihilating the navy, neutralizing proxies, preventing a nuclear weapon, and inviting Iranians to take over their government — that clarity was obscured and most were unattainable with the committed resources.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Objective proliferation is the diagnostic signature of a campaign with no defined success condition and therefore no natural stopping point.
insights.quote: The sheer number of U.S. objectives in Iran obscured any sense of clarity.
insights.locator: WHAT’S THIS WAR GOOD FOR?

insights.claim: The self-imposed prohibition on deploying ground forces made most of the stated objectives unachievable, creating a structural mismatch between ends and means.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Standoff-only campaigns cannot deliver regime or territorial outcomes, which bounds what any negotiated settlement can contain.
insights.locator: Moreover, many of those objectives were clearly unattainable

insights.claim: Trump's own claim that the June 2025 strikes had 'completely obliterated' Iran's nuclear program undercuts the rationale for the 2026 campaign, and the 2025 mission was halted before battle damage assessments that ultimately found only a one-to-two-year setback.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Official damage claims were contradicted by assessment; treat public battle-damage statements from this administration as unreliable inputs.
insights.quote: the mission in June 2025 was halted in advance of battle damage assessments and was not restarted after those assessments concluded that the program had set back the Iranian program by only a year or two

insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Financial escalation remains an unspent lever, so further sanctions or financial-system action against Iran is a live tail risk.

insights.claim: Iran's regime was at its weakest in decades before the war — weeks earlier, water shortages and economic deprivation had triggered mass protests suppressed by killing tens of thousands of Iranians — yet Trump never made the case for regime change as a vital interest.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: Attacking at the moment of maximum internal fragility produced consolidation rather than collapse, an outcome consistent with rally-round-the-flag dynamics.

insights.claim: Policy reassessment has degenerated into daily reversal rather than deliberate adjustment, exemplified by Trump imposing and repealing a 20 percent surcharge on Strait of Hormuz shipping within a single day, undermining 250 years of U.S. commitment to freedom of navigation.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: A U.S. administration willing to tax Hormuz transit even briefly is a new and underpriced policy risk for shipping and insurance markets.
insights.quote: Within the span of a single day, Trump imposed and then repealed a 20 percent surcharge on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, undermining 250 years of U.S. commitment to the freedom of navigation.

themes.theme: Costs, escalation, and the Hormuz shock

insights.claim: Administration planning did not encompass Iran's closure of the Strait of Hormuz — an act the author calls fatal to U.S. success — which also prevented the United States and allies from stockpiling fuel to mitigate economic disruption.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: The absence of pre-positioned fuel reserves means the energy price impact was amplified by planning failure, not just by the closure itself.

insights.claim: Hegseth claimed on July 21 that the war had cost $37.5 billion, budgeting expert Elaine McCusker puts the true figure above $50 billion, and the administration has requested an additional $88 billion supplemental that the author calls poorly justified.
insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: An $88 billion supplemental on top of $50-plus billion spent is the fiscal scale of the war and the specific vote where Congress holds leverage.

insights.speaker: Kori Schake
insights.so_what: A maximally concessive agreement still failed to hold, which sets a low prior on any near-term negotiated settlement sticking.

insights.so_what: A structural shift in the U.S.-Gulf bargain that should show up in Gulf hedging toward China and in base-access negotiations.

insights.so_what: An unprecedented bicameral rebuke, even if reversed, marks the first real crack in congressional acquiescence and a leading indicator of funding risk.
